title: This man receives sinners (Luke 15:1–10)
hook: grumbling leads to three stories of lost things found

segments.voice: Yesterday, a half-built tower and the advice to count the cost before you start. What did your counting show you? Day five hundred fifty-seven.

Luke chapter fifteen may be the most famous chapter he wrote. A lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. Most people know at least one of those stories. Fewer remember why Jesus told them. They weren't bedtime stories, and they weren't told to a quiet audience. They were his answer to a complaint, overheard at the edge of a crowd. It starts with two sentences that set up everything after them. And the complaint itself, said with a sneer, turned out to be one of the truest things anyone ever said about him.

In the King James Bible: "Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." Publicans were tax collectors, working with the Roman occupation, often seen as traitors and cheats. Sharing a table, in that world, meant accepting someone. So the worry was serious: what does it say about a teacher, about God, if he eats with these people? The Greek word for murmured is a grumbling, muttering word. It's the same word family used in the old Greek version of Exodus, when Israel grumbled in the wilderness. Jesus doesn't argue. He tells three stories, and the stakes keep rising. A shepherd loses one sheep out of a hundred. A woman loses one coin out of ten. Tomorrow, a father loses one son out of two. One percent, ten percent, half. And look at how each of the first two ends. Not with the finding. With a party. The shepherd calls his friends and neighbors: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost." The woman does the same: "Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost." Then Jesus says it straight: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." Here's the twist. The grumblers aren't the villains of these stories. They're being invited. Every story ends with someone saying come and celebrate with me. The question underneath the chapter is simple. When the lost come home, will you come to the party? This man receives sinners. It was meant as an accusation. Many Christians hear it as the best news in the book.
screen: `ONE IN A HUNDRED, ONE IN TEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice over someone's return. Settle and breathe. Think of someone who has come back: to health, to sobriety, to the family table, to faith, to talking to you after a long silence. Maybe the return was small and nobody marked it. Picture them clearly. Notice if any part of you is still grumbling, still keeping a list of what they did while they were gone. Let it be there. Then try, just for a moment, to feel the shepherd's joy instead. If you pray, you can give thanks for their return. The bell holds the time.
This man receives sinners. A grumbling accusation that sets up three stories of lost things found, each ending in a party.
Your line: joy in heaven. Today, tell the person who came back that you're glad, out loud, with no list attached. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians read Luke 15 often, especially in Lent, and many churches mark returns with celebration: welcoming people back to communion, to membership, or into recovery communities that meet in church halls.

what it means: Jesus' reply to people grumbling that he eats with sinners, ending each time with an invitation to the party.
what a scholar hears: the murmuring word echoes Israel in the wilderness, and the stakes rise from one in a hundred to one in two.
